claim: YOD1 (OTUD2) is a novel interactor of TRAF6 in human cells.
source: Here, we identified the deubiquitinating enzyme YOD1 (OTUD2) as a novel interactor of TRAF6 in human cells.
evidence: Supported by yeast-two-hybrid assays, pull-down experiments, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: YOD1 binds to the C-terminal TRAF homology domain of TRAF6.
source: YOD1 binds to the C-terminal TRAF homology domain of TRAF6 that also serves as the interaction surface for the adaptor p62/Sequestosome-1, which is required for IL-1 signaling to NF-κB.
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down experiments with recombinant proteins and co-immunoprecipitation with TRAF6 deletion constructs in Figure 1B, 1D.

claim: YOD1 competes with p62 for TRAF6 association.
source: We show that YOD1 competes with p62 for TRAF6 association and abolishes the sequestration of TRAF6 to cytosolic p62 aggregates by a non-catalytic mechanism.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing decreased p62/TRAF6 binding in the presence of YOD1 (Figure 3D, 3E) and microscopy data (Figure 3F).

claim: YOD1 abolishes the sequestration of TRAF6 to cytosolic p62 aggregates by a non-catalytic mechanism.
source: We show that YOD1 competes with p62 for TRAF6 association and abolishes the sequestration of TRAF6 to cytosolic p62 aggregates by a non-catalytic mechanism.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy showing that catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S also prevents TRAF6 recruitment to p62 aggregates (Figure 3F).

claim: YOD1 associates with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells but is released upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: YOD1 associates with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells but is released upon IL-1β stimulation, thereby facilitating TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination as well as NEMO/IKKγ substrate ubiquitination.
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HeLa cells and HUVEC demonstrating decreased YOD1/TRAF6 interaction after IL-1β stimulation (Figure 5D, Figure 7C, 7D).

claim: YOD1 release from TRAF6 upon IL-1β stimulation facilitates TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination.
source: YOD1 associates with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells but is released upon IL-1β stimulation, thereby facilitating TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination as well as NEMO/IKKγ substrate ubiquitination.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased TRAF6 ubiquitination in YOD1 knock-down cells (Figure 7E) and decreased ubiquitination upon YOD1 reconstitution (Figure 7B).

claim: YOD1 release from TRAF6 upon IL-1β stimulation facilitates NEMO/IKKγ substrate ubiquitination.
source: YOD1 associates with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells but is released upon IL-1β stimulation, thereby facilitating TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination as well as NEMO/IKKγ substrate ubiquitination.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased NEMO ubiquitination in YOD1 knock-down cells after IL-1β stimulation (Figure 7F).

claim: IL-1 triggered IKK/NF-κB signaling is decreased by YOD1 overexpression.
source: Further, IL-1 triggered IKK/NF-κB signaling and induction of target genes is decreased by YOD1 overexpression and augmented after YOD1 depletion.
evidence: Shown by reduced NF-κB target gene expression in YOD1 overexpressing HeLa cells (Figure 4C) and reduced NF-κB activation in YOD1 reconstituted cells (Figure 5F).

claim: IL-1 triggered IKK/NF-κB signaling is augmented after YOD1 depletion.
source: Further, IL-1 triggered IKK/NF-κB signaling and induction of target genes is decreased by YOD1 overexpression and augmented after YOD1 depletion.
evidence: Demonstrated by enhanced NF-κB target gene expression (Figure 4F), increased NF-κB DNA binding (Figure 4G, Figure 6A), and enhanced IκBα phosphorylation/degradation (Figure 6C) in YOD1 knock-down cells.

claim: YOD1 antagonizes TRAF6/p62-dependent IL-1 signaling to NF-κB.
source: Hence, our data define that YOD1 antagonizes TRAF6/p62-dependent IL-1 signaling to NF-κB.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing YOD1 competes with p62, prevents TRAF6 ubiquitination enhancement by p62, and negatively regulates IL-1-induced NF-κB activation.

claim: TRAF6 is an essential component to initiate IL-1R downstream signaling.
source: In turn, IRAK1, 2 and 3 interact with the E3 ligase TNF-receptor associated factor 6 (TRAF6), which is an essential component to initiate IL-1R downstream signaling (Ye et al., 2002; Cao et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Ye et al., 2002; Cao et al., 1996).

claim: TRAF6 bridges the Myddosome to TAK1 that acts as an IKKβ upstream kinase on the route to NF-κB.
source: TRAF6 bridges the Myddosome to TAK1 that acts as an IKKβ upstream kinase on the route to NF-κB (Lomaga et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2001; Sato et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Lomaga et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2001; Sato et al., 2005).

claim: TRAF6 belongs to the TRAF family of proteins that share a C-terminal TRAF region, consisting of coiled-coil and MATH domains.
source: TRAF6 belongs to the TRAF family of proteins that share a C-terminal TRAF region, consisting of coiled-coil and MATH (Meprin and TRAF homology) domains, which are needed for oligomerization and adaptor function (Ha et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Ha et al., 2009) and established knowledge of TRAF protein structure.

claim: The C-terminal TRAF region coiled-coil and MATH domains are needed for oligomerization and adaptor function.
source: TRAF6 belongs to the TRAF family of proteins that share a C-terminal TRAF region, consisting of coiled-coil and MATH (Meprin and TRAF homology) domains, which are needed for oligomerization and adaptor function (Ha et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Ha et al., 2009).

claim: The N-terminal RING and Zinc Finger1 (Z1) domain of TRAF6 confers ubiquitin ligase activity.
source: The N-terminal RING and Zinc Finger1 (Z1) domain confers ubiquitin ligase activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TRAF6 structure-function relationships.

claim: In response to IL-1 stimulation, TRAF6 in conjunction with the E2 enzyme UBC13/UEV1A catalyzes the attachment of lysine (K)63-linked ubiquitin chains to substrate proteins.
source: In response to IL-1 stimulation, TRAF6 in conjunction with the E2 enzyme UBC13/UEV1A catalyzes the attachment of lysine (K)63-linked ubiquitin chains to substrate proteins, including TRAF6 itself, IRAK1, TAK1 and the non-catalytic IKK complex component NEMO/IKKγ (Deng et al., 2000; Conze et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2010; Yamazaki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Deng et al., 2000; Conze et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2010; Yamazaki et al., 2009).

claim: TRAF6 catalyzes the attachment of K63-linked ubiquitin chains to TRAF6 itself, IRAK1, TAK1 and NEMO/IKKγ.
source: In response to IL-1 stimulation, TRAF6 in conjunction with the E2 enzyme UBC13/UEV1A catalyzes the attachment of lysine (K)63-linked ubiquitin chains to substrate proteins, including TRAF6 itself, IRAK1, TAK1 and the non-catalytic IKK complex component NEMO/IKKγ (Deng et al., 2000; Conze et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2010; Yamazaki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Deng et al., 2000; Conze et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2010; Yamazaki et al., 2009).

claim: TRAF6 E3 ligase activity is critical for activation of NF-κB signaling in response to IL-1.
source: Reconstitution experiments reveal that TRAF6 E3 ligase activity is critical for activation of NF-κB signaling in response to IL-1 (Lamothe et al., 2007; Walsh et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Lamothe et al., 2007; Walsh et al., 2008).

claim: TRAF6 overexpression alone is sufficient to strongly activate NF-κB.
source: Since TRAF6 overexpression alone is sufficient to strongly activate NF-κB (Cao et al., 1996), its activity needs to be tightly controlled by positive and negative regulators.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Cao et al., 1996).

claim: p62 is essential for TRAF6-dependent canonical NF-κB signaling and activation in response to IL-1 stimulation.
source: The atypical PKC-interacting protein p62 (also called Sequestosome-1; SQSTM-1) is essential for TRAF6-dependent canonical NF-κB signaling and activation in response to IL-1 stimulation (Sanz et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Sanz et al., 2000).

claim: p62 has been implicated in TRAF6-dependent signaling pathways emanating from CD40, RANK or NGF.
source: p62 has also been implicated in other TRAF6-dependent signaling pathways emanating from CD40, RANK or NGF (Wooten et al., 2005; Durán et al., 2004; Seibold and Ehrenschwender, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Wooten et al., 2005; Durán et al., 2004; Seibold and Ehrenschwender, 2015).

claim: TRAF6 is recruited to p62 aggresomes and p62 promotes TRAF6 E3 ligase activity to enhance auto- and substrate ubiquitination.
source: TRAF6 is recruited to p62 aggresomes and p62 promotes TRAF6 E3 ligase activity to enhance auto- and substrate ubiquitination (Sanz et al., 2000; Zotti et al., 2014; Wooten et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Sanz et al., 2000; Zotti et al., 2014; Wooten et al., 2005).

claim: p62 recruits the deubiquitinating enzyme CYLD that acts as negative regulator of NF-κB signaling.
source: However, p62 also recruits the deubiquitinating enzyme (DUB) CYLD (Cylindromatosis) that acts as negative regulator of NF-κB signaling (Jin et al., 2008; Wooten et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Jin et al., 2008; Wooten et al., 2008).

claim: CYLD cleaves K63-linked ubiquitin chains conjugated to TRAF6 and its substrates.
source: CYLD cleaves K63-linked ubiquitin chains conjugated to TRAF6 and its substrates (Yoshida et al., 2005; Reiley et al., 2007), revealing that it counteracts signaling by a catalytic mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Yoshida et al., 2005; Reiley et al., 2007).

claim: A20 counterbalances TRAF6 activity.
source: Besides CYLD, the ubiquitin editing enzyme A20 counterbalances TRAF6 activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: After prolonged IL-1 stimulation A20 binds to TRAF6 to prevent TRAF6/UBC13 interaction by a process independent of its DUB activity.
source: After pro-longed IL-1 stimulation A20 binds to TRAF6 to prevent TRAF6/UBC13 interaction by a process independent of its DUB activity (Shembade et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Shembade et al., 2010).

claim: YOD1 is a homolog of yeast OTU1.
source: Here, we report on the identification of the OTU (ovarian tumor) DUB family member YOD1 (homolog of yeast OTU1; OTUD2, DUBA8) as a new interactor of TRAF6.
evidence: Based on established nomenclature and sequence homology.

claim: The yeast homolog OTU1 acts as a cofactor of the hexameric AAA-ATPase Cdc48/p97 for protein processing.
source: Originally, the yeast homolog OTU1 was shown to act as a cofactor of the hexameric AAA-ATPase Cdc48/p97 for protein processing (Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006).

claim: In mammalian cells, YOD1 facilitates protein quality control by VCP/p97 at the endoplasmic reticulum through the ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) pathway.
source: In mammalian cells, YOD1 facilitates protein quality control by Valosin-containing protein (VCP)/p97 at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through the ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) pathway (Claessen et al., 2010; Ernst et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Claessen et al., 2010; Ernst et al., 2009).

claim: YOD1 directly associates with TRAF6.
source: We find that YOD1 directly associates with TRAF6 and competes with p62 for TRAF6 binding and activation.
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down experiments with recombinant proteins (Figure 1B) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1C-K).

claim: YOD1 depletion enhances canonical NF-κB activation.
source: YOD1 is released from TRAF6 upon IL-1 stimulation and YOD1 depletion enhances canonical NF-κB activation.
evidence: Demonstrated by enhanced NF-κB DNA binding, IκBα phosphorylation/degradation, and target gene expression in YOD1 knock-down cells (Figure 4F-H, Figure 6A-C).

claim: YOD1 is a novel negative regulator of TRAF6/p62-triggered IL-1 signaling.
source: These results define YOD1 as novel negative regulator of TRAF6/p62-triggered IL-1 signaling.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing YOD1 inhibits IL-1-induced NF-κB signaling and competes with p62 for TRAF6 binding.

claim: YOD1 interacts with full length TRAF6 in yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: We discovered a novel interaction of YOD1 with full length TRAF6, but not with a fragment comprising the catalytic RING-Zinc Finger1 (Z1) domain (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid growth assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: YOD1 does not interact with a TRAF6 fragment comprising the catalytic RING-Zinc Finger1 (Z1) domain.
source: We discovered a novel interaction of YOD1 with full length TRAF6, but not with a fragment comprising the catalytic RING-Zinc Finger1 (Z1) domain (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mammalian YOD1 and its yeast homolog OTU1 were identified as co-factor of the AAA-ATPase p97/Cdc48.
source: Originally, mammalian YOD1 and its yeast homolog OTU1 were identified as co-factor of the AAA-ATPase p97/Cdc48 (Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006; Ernst et al., 2009), which was also confirmed in the Y2H (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006; Ernst et al., 2009) and confirmed by yeast two-hybrid data in Figure 1A.

claim: TRAF6 self-associates in yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Besides the binding to YOD1, TRAF6 self-associated and bound to the E2 enzyme UBC13 and the ubiquitin editing enzyme A20, but not to p97 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRAF6 binds to the E2 enzyme UBC13 in yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Besides the binding to YOD1, TRAF6 self-associated and bound to the E2 enzyme UBC13 and the ubiquitin editing enzyme A20, but not to p97 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRAF6 binds to the ubiquitin editing enzyme A20 in yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Besides the binding to YOD1, TRAF6 self-associated and bound to the E2 enzyme UBC13 and the ubiquitin editing enzyme A20, but not to p97 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRAF6 does not bind to p97 in yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Besides the binding to YOD1, TRAF6 self-associated and bound to the E2 enzyme UBC13 and the ubiquitin editing enzyme A20, but not to p97 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: YOD1 shows weak interaction with cIAP2 and SHARPIN in yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Despite some weak interaction with cIAP2 and SHARPIN, within this panel YOD1 was quite selectively binding to p97 and TRAF6.
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YOD1 selectively binds to p97 and TRAF6 within a panel of E3 ligases and ubiquitin system proteins.
source: Despite some weak interaction with cIAP2 and SHARPIN, within this panel YOD1 was quite selectively binding to p97 and TRAF6.
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YOD1 is a direct interactor of the TRAF6 C-terminus in vitro.
source: Clearly, YOD1 was binding to the C-terminal MATH (346 -504) but not to the N-terminal RING-Z1 (50–159) domain of TRAF6.
evidence: Demonstrated by GST pull-down experiments with recombinant proteins shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: YOD1 does not bind to the N-terminal RING-Z1 domain of TRAF6 in vitro.
source: Clearly, YOD1 was binding to the C-terminal MATH (346 -504) but not to the N-terminal RING-Z1 (50–159) domain of TRAF6.
evidence: Demonstrated by GST pull-down experiments with recombinant proteins shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: YOD1 binds to p97 in vitro.
source: In addition, we confirmed binding of recombinant YOD1 to p97 by GST-PD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by GST pull-down experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: YOD1-p97 association is not prevented by TRAF6.
source: In a triple PD experiment we neither found that YOD1-p97 association was prevented by TRAF6 nor that p97 did influence interaction of YOD1 to the TRAF6 MATH domain, revealing that both proteins can bind to YOD1 independently (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by triple pull-down experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: p97 does not influence interaction of YOD1 to the TRAF6 MATH domain.
source: In a triple PD experiment we neither found that YOD1-p97 association was prevented by TRAF6 nor that p97 did influence interaction of YOD1 to the TRAF6 MATH domain, revealing that both proteins can bind to YOD1 independently (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by triple pull-down experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: TRAF6 and p97 can bind to YOD1 independently.
source: In a triple PD experiment we neither found that YOD1-p97 association was prevented by TRAF6 nor that p97 did influence interaction of YOD1 to the TRAF6 MATH domain, revealing that both proteins can bind to YOD1 independently (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Inferred from triple pull-down experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C demonstrating no mutual interference.

claim: YOD1 and TRAF6 interact in HEK293 cells.
source: To investigate whether YOD1 and TRAF6 also interact in cells, we co-expressed full length FLAG-YOD1 and HA-TRAF6 in HEK293 cells. Co-immunoprecipitations (IP) using anti-HA or anti-FLAG antibodies confirmed the interaction of TRAF6 and YOD1 (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: YOD1 binds to the C-terminal MATH domain but not to the N-terminal RING-Z1-Z4 region of TRAF6 in cells.
source: Congruent with the Y2H and PD results, YOD1 bound to the C-terminal MATH domain, but not to the N-terminal RING-Z1-Z4 region of TRAF6 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation with TRAF6 deletion constructs shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The N-terminal UBX domain of YOD1 is essential to mediate TRAF6 interaction.
source: On the side of YOD1, the N-terminal UBX domain was essential to mediate TRAF6 interaction (Figure 1E, scheme Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation with YOD1 deletion constructs shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A putative TRAF6 interaction motif exists within the UBX domain of YOD1.
source: Sequence comparison indicated the existence of a putative TRAF6 interaction motif (TIM) for MATH interactors within the UBX domain (PXEXXAr/Ac) (Ye et al., 2002) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and comparison to known TIM consensus (Ye et al., 2002).

claim: Binding of TRAF6 MATH to YOD1 UBX domain is not mediated through a typical TIM.
source: However, neither exchange of the conserved glutamic acid to alanine (YOD1 E96A) nor even more profound mutations of the putative TRAF6 binding motif abolished YOD1 association (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that binding of TRAF6 MATH to YOD1 UBX domain is not mediated through a typical TIM.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with YOD1 mutants shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: YOD1 does not bind to TRAF2.
source: We did not detect YOD1-TRAF2 binding, indicating a selectivity of YOD1 for association with TRAF6.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: YOD1 shows selectivity for association with TRAF6 over TRAF2.
source: We did not detect YOD1-TRAF2 binding, indicating a selectivity of YOD1 for association with TRAF6.
evidence: Inferred from lack of YOD1-TRAF2 binding shown in Figure 1G compared to YOD1-TRAF6 binding.

claim: Endogenous YOD1 co-precipitates with endogenous TRAF6 in HEK293 cells.
source: Indeed, in all cell lines and primary HUVEC YOD1 was specifically co-precipitating with endogenous TRAF6, as validated by either TRAF6 or YOD1 IP.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation of endogenous proteins shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Endogenous YOD1 co-precipitates with endogenous TRAF6 in HeLa cells.
source: Indeed, in all cell lines and primary HUVEC YOD1 was specifically co-precipitating with endogenous TRAF6, as validated by either TRAF6 or YOD1 IP.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation of endogenous proteins shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Endogenous YOD1 co-precipitates with endogenous TRAF6 in U2OS cells.
source: Indeed, in all cell lines and primary HUVEC YOD1 was specifically co-precipitating with endogenous TRAF6, as validated by either TRAF6 or YOD1 IP.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation of endogenous proteins shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Endogenous YOD1 co-precipitates with endogenous TRAF6 in primary HUVEC.
source: Indeed, in all cell lines and primary HUVEC YOD1 was specifically co-precipitating with endogenous TRAF6, as validated by either TRAF6 or YOD1 IP.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation of endogenous proteins shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Specificity of TRAF6/YOD1 interaction is confirmed by decreased co-precipitation of YOD1 in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells.
source: Further, specificity of TRAF6/YOD1 interaction was confirmed by the decreased co-precipitation of YOD1 in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in TRAF6 knock-down cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: YOD1/TRAF6 binding is not significantly altered upon p97 depletion.
source: Since YOD1 has been described as a cellular co-factor of p97, we checked for YOD1/TRAF6 interaction in p97 knock-down HEK293 cells and found that binding of YOD1 to TRAF6 was not significantly altered upon p97 depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in p97 knock-down cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: RFP-TRAF6 is distributed in small dots in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus when overexpressed in U2OS cells.
source: Whereas RFP-TRAF6 was distributed in small dots in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus, GFP-YOD1 and catalytically inactive GFP-YOD1 C160S were evenly dispersed in the cytoplasm and nucleus with some accumulations in or around the nucleus (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GFP-YOD1 is evenly dispersed in the cytoplasm and nucleus with some accumulations in or around the nucleus when overexpressed in U2OS cells.
source: Whereas RFP-TRAF6 was distributed in small dots in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus, GFP-YOD1 and catalytically inactive GFP-YOD1 C160S were evenly dispersed in the cytoplasm and nucleus with some accumulations in or around the nucleus (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Catalytically inactive GFP-YOD1 C160S is evenly dispersed in the cytoplasm and nucleus with some accumulations in or around the nucleus when overexpressed in U2OS cells.
source: Whereas RFP-TRAF6 was distributed in small dots in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus, GFP-YOD1 and catalytically inactive GFP-YOD1 C160S were evenly dispersed in the cytoplasm and nucleus with some accumulations in or around the nucleus (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP-YOD1 and RFP-TRAF6 co-localize to cytosolic speckles upon co-expression in U2OS cells.
source: Upon co-expression, GFP-YOD1 and RFP-TRAF6 were to a large extent co-localizing to cytosolic speckles, indicating that the proteins interact inside the cell and can form larger clusters (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy and plot profile analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: YOD1 and TRAF6 interact inside the cell and can form larger clusters.
source: Upon co-expression, GFP-YOD1 and RFP-TRAF6 were to a large extent co-localizing to cytosolic speckles, indicating that the proteins interact inside the cell and can form larger clusters (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Inferred from co-localization data shown in Figure 2B and quantitative analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The RFP-TRAF6 signal is enriched in GFP-YOD1 spots and vice versa the GFP-YOD1 signal is enhanced in RFP-TRAF6 spots.
source: Compared to the background, the RFP-TRAF6 signal was enriched in GFP-YOD1 spots and vice versa the GFP-YOD1 signal was enhanced in RFP-TRAF6 spots, clearly suggesting co-localization of TRAF6 and YOD1 in the clusters.
evidence: Demonstrated by automated image analysis of fluorescence intensities shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Interaction of TRAF6 and YOD1 does not rely on YOD1 catalytic activity.
source: Interaction of TRAF6 and YOD1 did not rely on YOD1 catalytic activity, because like YOD1 WT, the DUB mutant YOD1 C160S was co-localizing (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and co-precipitating with TRAF6 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-localization (Figure 2B) and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 2C) experiments with catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S.

claim: Crimson-p62 forms punctuated aggregates when expressed in U2OS cells.
source: As expected, we observed similar aggregates when Crimson-p62 was expressed in U2OS cells (Figure 3A)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TRAF6 is recruited to p62 sequestosomes in U2OS cells.
source: and TRAF6 was recruited to the punctuated p62 sequestosomes in U2OS cells as evident from plotted FI of CFP-p62 and RFP-TRAF6 spots as well as co-clustering of FI as measured by automated image analysis (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy, plot profile analysis, and automated image analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP-YOD1 does not co-localize with Crimson-p62 aggregates.
source: In contrast, GFP-YOD1 was not co-localizing with Crimson-p62 aggregates.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: p62 staining appears slightly more diffuse in YOD1 expressing cells.
source: However, it appeared that p62 staining was slightly more diffuse in YOD1 expressing cells, hinting at an indirect effect of YOD1 on the formation of p62 sequestosomes (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Observed in confocal fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: p62 binds to FLAG-TRAF6 but not to FLAG-YOD1 in HEK293 cells.
source: We confirmed by co-IP that p62 binds to FLAG-TRAF6, but not to FLAG-YOD1 in HEK293 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YOD1 and p62 both bind to the C-terminal MATH domain of TRAF6.
source: By directly comparing the binding of YOD1 and p62 to TRAF6 in HEK293 cells we could confirm that both proteins are associating with the C-terminal MATH domain (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation with TRAF6 deletion constructs shown in Figure 3C.

claim: YOD1 inhibits the association of TRAF6 and p62.
source: Indeed, co-IP experiments using MYC-TRAF6 together with Crimson-p62 and GFP-YOD1 revealed that YOD1 was able to inhibit the association of TRAF6 and p62, while p62 did not alter the binding of YOD1 to TRAF6 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3D and quantified in Figure 3E.

claim: p62 does not alter the binding of YOD1 to TRAF6.
source: Indeed, co-IP experiments using MYC-TRAF6 together with Crimson-p62 and GFP-YOD1 revealed that YOD1 was able to inhibit the association of TRAF6 and p62, while p62 did not alter the binding of YOD1 to TRAF6 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3D and quantified in Figure 3E.

claim: Inhibition of p62/TRAF6 binding by YOD1 is independent of YOD1 catalytic activity.
source: Inhibition of p62/TRAF6 binding was independent of YOD1 catalytic activity, suggesting that YOD1 and p62 are competing for an association with TRAF6 independent of YOD1 DUB activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by similar inhibition with catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: YOD1 and p62 are competing for an association with TRAF6 independent of YOD1 DUB activity.
source: Inhibition of p62/TRAF6 binding was independent of YOD1 catalytic activity, suggesting that YOD1 and p62 are competing for an association with TRAF6 independent of YOD1 DUB activity.
evidence: Inferred from data showing catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S also inhibits p62/TRAF6 binding (Figure 3D, 3E).

claim: YOD1 and TRAF6 co-localize within clusters while p62 is largely excluded from YOD1/TRAF6 aggregates when all three proteins are co-expressed.
source: Even though all three proteins were found in cytoplasmic speckles, the merged images especially at a higher magnification indicated that while YOD1 and TRAF6 were co-localizing within clusters as seen in the absence of Crimson-p62 (see Figure 2B), p62 in contrast was in the vicinity, but largely excluded from YOD1/TRAF6 aggregates.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy and plot profile analysis shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S shows the same distribution as YOD1 WT when co-expressed with TRAF6 and p62.
source: The same distribution was seen when catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S was expressed in U2OS cells (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Automated image analysis shows stronger enrichment of RFP-TRAF6 signal in GFP-YOD1 spots compared to Crimson-p62 spots.
source: Also, automated image analysis of FI in a larger number of cells indicates a stronger enrichment of RFP-TRAF6 signal in GFP-YOD1 spots compared to Crimson-p62 spots and no co-localization beyond background of Crimson-p62 in RFP-TRAF6 or GFP-YOD1 clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by automated fluorescence imaging analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: YOD1, p62 and TRAF6 are not found in a trimeric complex.
source: Thus, co-IP and co-localization studies suggest that YOD1, p62 and TRAF6 are not found in a trimeric complex, but that YOD1 and p62 compete for TRAF6 association and that YOD1 can interfere with the recruitment of TRAF6 to p62 sequestosomes by a non-catalytic mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and co-localization data showing competitive binding and spatial exclusion (Figure 3D-F).

claim: YOD1 can interfere with the recruitment of TRAF6 to p62 sequestosomes by a non-catalytic mechanism.
source: Thus, co-IP and co-localization studies suggest that YOD1, p62 and TRAF6 are not found in a trimeric complex, but that YOD1 and p62 compete for TRAF6 association and that YOD1 can interfere with the recruitment of TRAF6 to p62 sequestosomes by a non-catalytic mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from data showing catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S also prevents TRAF6 recruitment to p62 aggregates (Figure 3F).

claim: Expression of YOD1 WT causes a significant decline in NF-κB target gene induction after IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
source: While DOX treatment alone did not significantly alter expression of these genes in HeLa parental cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), expression of YOD1 WT or C160S caused a significant decline in NF-κB target gene induction after IL-1β stimulation, indicating that YOD1 can antagonize IL-1R triggered NF-κB signaling independent of its catalytic activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis of NF-κB target genes in YOD1 overexpressing cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of YOD1 C160S causes a significant decline in NF-κB target gene induction after IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
source: While DOX treatment alone did not significantly alter expression of these genes in HeLa parental cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), expression of YOD1 WT or C160S caused a significant decline in NF-κB target gene induction after IL-1β stimulation, indicating that YOD1 can antagonize IL-1R triggered NF-κB signaling independent of its catalytic activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis of NF-κB target genes in YOD1 C160S overexpressing cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: YOD1 can antagonize IL-1R triggered NF-κB signaling independent of its catalytic activity.
source: While DOX treatment alone did not significantly alter expression of these genes in HeLa parental cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), expression of YOD1 WT or C160S caused a significant decline in NF-κB target gene induction after IL-1β stimulation, indicating that YOD1 can antagonize IL-1R triggered NF-κB signaling independent of its catalytic activity.
evidence: Inferred from similar effects of YOD1 WT and catalytically inactive C160S on NF-κB target gene expression (Figure 4C).

claim: YOD1 knock-down results in enhanced NF-κB target gene expression after IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
source: In line with a negative regulatory function of YOD1 for IL-1β signaling to NF-κB, reduction of YOD1 resulted in enhanced NF-κB target gene expression, which was especially evident at early stimulation time points.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 4F.

claim: YOD1 counteracts a rapid induction of NF-κB target genes in response to IL-1β stimulation.
source: Taken together, overexpression and knock-down experiments suggest that YOD1 counteracts a rapid induction of NF-κB target genes in response to IL-1β stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from overexpression experiments showing decreased target gene expression (Figure 4C) and knock-down experiments showing enhanced expression (Figure 4F).

claim: Decreased TRAF6 expression severely reduces NF-κB activation and target gene expression upon IL-1β stimulation in iBMDM.
source: As expected, decreased TRAF6 expression severely reduced NF-κB activation and target gene expression upon IL-1β stimulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA, Western blot, and qRT-PCR in TRAF6 knock-down iBMDM shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: Diminished expression of YOD1 augments IκBα phosphorylation/degradation in iBMDM upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: In contrast, diminished expression of YOD1 augmented IκBα phosphorylation/degradation as well as NF-κB DNA binding and enhanced the expression of TNFAIP3/A20 and NFKBIA/IκBα, revealing that YOD1 counteracts IL-1β triggered NF-κB signaling in iBMDM.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis in YOD1 knock-down iBMDM shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Diminished expression of YOD1 augments NF-κB DNA binding in iBMDM upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: In contrast, diminished expression of YOD1 augmented IκBα phosphorylation/degradation as well as NF-κB DNA binding and enhanced the expression of TNFAIP3/A20 and NFKBIA/IκBα, revealing that YOD1 counteracts IL-1β triggered NF-κB signaling in iBMDM.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in YOD1 knock-down iBMDM shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Diminished expression of YOD1 enhances the expression of TNFAIP3/A20 and NFKBIA/IκBα in iBMDM upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: In contrast, diminished expression of YOD1 augmented IκBα phosphorylation/degradation as well as NF-κB DNA binding and enhanced the expression of TNFAIP3/A20 and NFKBIA/IκBα, revealing that YOD1 counteracts IL-1β triggered NF-κB signaling in iBMDM.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in YOD1 knock-down iBMDM shown in Figure 4H.

claim: YOD1 counteracts IL-1β triggered NF-κB signaling in iBMDM.
source: In contrast, diminished expression of YOD1 augmented IκBα phosphorylation/degradation as well as NF-κB DNA binding and enhanced the expression of TNFAIP3/A20 and NFKBIA/IκBα, revealing that YOD1 counteracts IL-1β triggered NF-κB signaling in iBMDM.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced NF-κB signaling and target gene expression in YOD1 knock-down iBMDM (Figure 4G, 4H).

claim: Two independent YOD1 KO HeLa cell clones (#6 and #33) were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
source: The approach yielded two independent HeLa cell clones (#6 and #33) that carry the expected genomic deletion as verified by sequencing.
evidence: Demonstrated by PCR, Western blot, and sequencing analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Reconstituted YOD1 binds to TRAF6 in unstimulated YOD1 KO cells.
source: Co-IP revealed binding of reconstituted YOD1 to TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was reduced after IL-1β stimulation (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5D.

claim: YOD1/TRAF6 interaction is reduced after IL-1β stimulation in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells.
source: Co-IP revealed binding of reconstituted YOD1 to TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was reduced after IL-1β stimulation (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation at different time points after IL-1β stimulation shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YOD1 reconstitution in YOD1 KO cells reduces NF-κB target gene expression after IL-1β stimulation.
source: On the level of NF-κB target gene expression we could verify the negative regulatory influence of YOD1 on gene induction as previously seen upon YOD1 overexpression or knock-down in HeLa cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Activation of NF-κB DNA binding in response to IL-1β stimulation is reduced in YOD1 expressing cells compared to YOD1 KO cells.
source: As expected for a putative negative regulator that controls TRAF6-dependent upstream signaling, activation of NF-κB DNA binding in response to IL-1β stimulation was reduced in YOD1 expressing HeLa cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα is reduced in YOD1 expressing cells compared to YOD1 KO cells after IL-1β stimulation.
source: In line, phosphorylation and degradation of the NF-κB inhibitor IκBα was reduced in YOD1 expressing cells (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Reconstitution of two independent YOD1 KO cell clones provides evidence that YOD1 counteracts NF-κB signaling upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: Thus, reconstitution of two independent KO cell clones provided clear evidence that YOD1 counteracts NF-κB signaling upon IL-1β stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from consistent results in two independent YOD1 KO clones showing reduced NF-κB signaling upon YOD1 reconstitution (Figure 5E, 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

claim: TRAF6 knock-down severely impairs IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation in HeLa cells.
source: Whereas knock-down of TRAF6 or p62 severely impaired IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation as evident by EMSA, depletion of YOD1 enhanced NF-κB activation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: p62 knock-down severely impairs IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation in HeLa cells.
source: Whereas knock-down of TRAF6 or p62 severely impaired IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation as evident by EMSA, depletion of YOD1 enhanced NF-κB activation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in p62 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: YOD1 depletion enhances IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation in HeLa cells.
source: Whereas knock-down of TRAF6 or p62 severely impaired IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation as evident by EMSA, depletion of YOD1 enhanced NF-κB activation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in YOD1 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 is decreased by TRAF6 knock-down in HeLa cells.
source: Congruently, induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 was decreased by TRAF6 or p62 knock-down and increased by YOD1 knock-down (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 is decreased by p62 knock-down in HeLa cells.
source: Congruently, induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 was decreased by TRAF6 or p62 knock-down and increased by YOD1 knock-down (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in p62 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 is increased by YOD1 knock-down in HeLa cells.
source: Congruently, induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 was decreased by TRAF6 or p62 knock-down and increased by YOD1 knock-down (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in YOD1 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TRAF6 knock-down prevents IκBα degradation upon IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
source: Downregulation of TRAF6 or p62 prevented IκBα degradation and YOD1 depletion enhanced IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation, demonstrating that all proteins affect NF-κB signaling (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: p62 knock-down prevents IκBα degradation upon IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
source: Downregulation of TRAF6 or p62 prevented IκBα degradation and YOD1 depletion enhanced IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation, demonstrating that all proteins affect NF-κB signaling (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in p62 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: YOD1 depletion enhances IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
source: Downregulation of TRAF6 or p62 prevented IκBα degradation and YOD1 depletion enhanced IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation, demonstrating that all proteins affect NF-κB signaling (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in YOD1 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: YOD1 controls IKK activation as YOD1 reduction coincides with increased IKK T-loop phosphorylation after IL-1β treatment.
source: Since TRAF6 acts upstream of IKK on the route to NF-κB, we verified that YOD1 also controls IKK activation by showing that YOD1 reduction coincides with increased IKK T-loop phosphorylation after IL-1β treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of IKK phosphorylation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: YOD1 knock-down does not affect the activation of the MAPKs JNK, p38 and ERK upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: Of note, while IKK/NF-κB activation was significantly enhanced in the absence of YOD1, we found no effect of YOD1 knock-down on the activation of the MAPKs JNK, p38 and ERK (Figure 6E).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of MAPK phosphorylation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TRAF6 is involved in NF-κB activation in response to IL-1R stimulation but dispensable for TNFR triggered NF-κB activation.
source: TRAF6 is involved in NF-κB activation in response to IL-1R stimulation, but dispensable for TNFR triggered NF-κB activation (Lomaga et al., 1999; Cao et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Lomaga et al., 1999; Cao et al., 1996).

claim: YOD1 depletion leads to strongly augmented NF-κB signaling and activation after IL-1R engagement but not after TNFα stimulation.
source: While both stimuli induced NF-κB activation as evident by IκBα degradation and NF-κB DNA binding, YOD1 depletion led to strongly augmented NF-κB signaling and activation after IL-1R engagement, while TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling was unaffected by altered YOD1 amounts.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA and Western blot comparing IL-1β and TNFα stimulation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6F.

claim: TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling is unaffected by altered YOD1 amounts.
source: While both stimuli induced NF-κB activation as evident by IκBα degradation and NF-κB DNA binding, YOD1 depletion led to strongly augmented NF-κB signaling and activation after IL-1R engagement, while TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling was unaffected by altered YOD1 amounts.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA and Western blot comparing IL-1β and TNFα stimulation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6F.

claim: YOD1 expression does not interfere with TRAF6 poly-ubiquitination under denaturing conditions.
source: Under denaturing conditions (1% SDS) and after MYC-IP, TRAF6 ubiquitination is readily detectable and YOD1 expression did not interfere with TRAF6 poly-ubiquitination, which is in line with its previously reported inability to cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains (Mevissen et al., 2013) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A and supported by citation to previous literature (Mevissen et al., 2013).

claim: YOD1 is unable to cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: Under denaturing conditions (1% SDS) and after MYC-IP, TRAF6 ubiquitination is readily detectable and YOD1 expression did not interfere with TRAF6 poly-ubiquitination, which is in line with its previously reported inability to cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains (Mevissen et al., 2013) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Mevissen et al., 2013) and confirmed by in vitro cleavage assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Binding of p62 enhances TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination.
source: Binding of p62 has been shown to enhance TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination (Wooten et al., 2005) and as expected, TRAF6 ubiquitination was strongly increased in the presence of p62 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Wooten et al., 2005) and demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-expression of YOD1 abrogates the enhancement of TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by p62.
source: Noticeably, co-expression of YOD1 abrogated this enhancement.
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S impairs the boost of TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by p62, though not as severely as YOD1 WT.
source: Also, catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S impaired the boost of TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by p62, even though the inhibition was not quite as severe as with YOD1 WT.
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Recombinant YOD1 does not cleave TRAF6 ubiquitin chains in vitro.
source: In contrast, neither recombinant YOD1 (K11, K27, K29 and K33 selectivity) nor Cezanne (K11 selectivity) were cleaving TRAF6 ubiquitin chains.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB cleavage assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: p62-induced attachment of K63-linked ubiquitin chains to TRAF6 is counterbalanced by YOD1 primarily by a non-catalytic mechanism.
source: Therefore, the data show that p62-induced attachment of K63-linked ubiquitin chains to TRAF6 is counterbalanced by YOD1 primarily by a non-catalytic mechanism that involves competition with p62 for TRAF6 association (compare Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Inferred from data showing YOD1 does not cleave K63 chains but competes with p62 for TRAF6 binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3E, 3F).

claim: TRAF6 ubiquitination upon IL-1β treatment is diminished upon re-expression of YOD1 in YOD1 KO cells.
source: TRAF6 was ubiquitinated upon IL-1β treatment in mock transduced YOD1 KO HeLa cell clones, but TRAF6 ubiquitination was diminished upon re-expression of YOD1 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IL-1-induced TRAF6 ubiquitination correlates with decreased binding of YOD1 to TRAF6 after IL-1 stimulation.
source: In fact, IL-1-induced TRAF6 ubiquitination correlates with a decreased binding of YOD1 to TRAF6 after IL-1 stimulation (see Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and we asked, whether reduced binding is also visible at the level of endogenous proteins in HeLa cells and primary HUVEC cells (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing time-dependent decrease in YOD1/TRAF6 interaction (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 7C, 7D).

claim: YOD1 co-precipitates with TRAF6 in unstimulated HeLa cells and the interaction is lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation.
source: As noted earlier, YOD1 was co-precipitating with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation, revealing that TRAF6 is released from YOD1.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation time course in HeLa cells shown in Figure 7C.

claim: YOD1 co-precipitates with TRAF6 in unstimulated HUVEC and the interaction is lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation.
source: As noted earlier, YOD1 was co-precipitating with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation, revealing that TRAF6 is released from YOD1.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation time course in HUVEC shown in Figure 7D.

claim: p62 depletion completely abolishes stimulus-dependent TRAF6 ubiquitination.
source: Whereas p62 depletion completely abolished stimulus-dependent TRAF6 ubiquitination, down-regulation of YOD1 had an opposite effect, leading to increased ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in p62 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Down-regulation of YOD1 leads to increased TRAF6 ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
source: Whereas p62 depletion completely abolished stimulus-dependent TRAF6 ubiquitination, down-regulation of YOD1 had an opposite effect, leading to increased ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7E.

claim: TRAF6 is primarily modified with K63-linked ubiquitin chains upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: However, none of the other DUBs including YOD1 was able to remove TRAF6 ubiquitin chains, strongly suggesting that TRAF6 is primarily modified with K63-linked ubiquitin chains and that YOD1 is counteracting TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by a non-catalytic mechanism.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB cleavage assay showing K63-specific DUBs cleave TRAF6 ubiquitin chains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).

claim: YOD1 is counteracting TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by a non-catalytic mechanism.
source: However, none of the other DUBs including YOD1 was able to remove TRAF6 ubiquitin chains, strongly suggesting that TRAF6 is primarily modified with K63-linked ubiquitin chains and that YOD1 is counteracting TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by a non-catalytic mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from inability of YOD1 to cleave TRAF6 ubiquitin chains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) combined with its ability to prevent p62-enhanced ubiquitination (Figure 7A).

claim: Ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment requires p62.
source: Ubiquitination of the IKK regulatory subunit NEMO is an important step in stimulus-dependent IKK activation and it was shown that NEMO ubiquitination induced by TRAF6 expression or IL-1β stimulation requires p62 (Zotti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Zotti et al., 2014).

claim: Ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment is abolished in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells.
source: Also in HeLa cells ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment was abolished in TRAF6 or p62 knock-down cells and YOD1 depletion had the opposite effect by enhancing stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7F).
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in TRAF6 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment is abolished in p62 knock-down HeLa cells.
source: Also in HeLa cells ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment was abolished in TRAF6 or p62 knock-down cells and YOD1 depletion had the opposite effect by enhancing stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7F).
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in p62 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7F.

claim: YOD1 depletion enhances stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
source: Also in HeLa cells ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment was abolished in TRAF6 or p62 knock-down cells and YOD1 depletion had the opposite effect by enhancing stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7F).
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7F.

claim: YOD1 counteracts IL-1 signaling to NF-κB by functioning as a negative regulator of TRAF6/p62-mediated ubiquitination events.
source: Thus, YOD1 counteracts IL-1 signaling to NF-κB by functioning as a negative regulator of TRAF6/p62-mediated ubiquitination events.
evidence: Inferred from data showing YOD1 prevents p62-enhanced TRAF6 ubiquitination and NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7A, 7E, 7F).

claim: YOD1 is an OTU domain DUB that can hydrolyze K11, K27, K29 and K33 ubiquitin linkages.
source: YOD1 is an OTU domain DUB that can hydrolyze K11, K27, K29 and K33 ubiquitin linkages (Mevissen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Mevissen et al., 2013).

claim: Structure-function analyses show a high preference of the YOD1 OTU for K11- and K33-linked ubiquitin.
source: Structure-function analyses showed a high preference of the YOD1 OTU for K11- and K33-linked ubiquitin (Flierman et al., 2016) and as expected, we do not detect cleavage of K63-linked ubiquitin chains generated by TRAF6.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Flierman et al., 2016) and confirmed by in vitro cleavage assay (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claim: CYLD is acting on TRAF6/p62 complexes but is not preventing the formation of TRAF6/p62 aggregates.
source: As we described here for YOD1, CYLD is acting on TRAF6/p62 complexes, but - in contrast to YOD1 - CYLD is not preventing the formation of TRAF6/p62 aggregates, but is recruited to TRAF6 by p62 (Jin et al., 2008; Wooten et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Jin et al., 2008; Wooten et al., 2008).

claim: CYLD is recruited to TRAF6 by p62 and hydrolyzes K63-linked ubiquitin chains generated by active TRAF6.
source: Upon recruitment, CYLD is hydrolyzing K63-linked ubiquitin chains generated by active TRAF6 (Wooten et al., 2008; Yoshida et al., 2005; Jin et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Wooten et al., 2008; Yoshida et al., 2005; Jin et al., 2008).

claim: A20 associates with TRAF6 only upon prolonged IL-1 stimulation to counteract binding of the E2 enzyme UBC13 to the RING-Z1 of TRAF6.
source: However, whereas YOD1 binds to TRAF6 in resting cells affecting C-terminal substrate binding, A20 is associating with TRAF6 only upon prolonged IL-1 stimulation to counteract binding of the E2 enzyme UBC13 to the RING-Z1 of TRAF6 (Shembade et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Shembade et al., 2010).

claim: CYLD and A20 act as negative feedback regulators that terminate post-inductive TRAF6 activity.
source: Thus, CYLD and A20 act as negative feedback regulators that terminate post-inductive TRAF6 activity by a catalytic or non-catalytic mechanism, respectively.
evidence: Inferred from the timing and mechanism of CYLD and A20 action on TRAF6 as described in previous literature.

claim: YOD1 acts in an earlier phase of the IL-1 response to counteract the accessibility of p62.
source: The YOD1/TRAF6 association in uninduced cells and the dissociation upon IL-1 stimulation indicate that YOD1 is acting in an earlier phase of the IL-1 response to counteract the accessibility of p62.
evidence: Inferred from data showing YOD1 binds TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and is released upon IL-1 stimulation (Figure 7C, 7D).

claim: Early NF-κB signaling and gene induction is increased upon YOD1 depletion.
source: In line, we show that early NF-κB signaling and gene induction is increased upon YOD1 depletion.
evidence: Demonstrated by enhanced NF-κB target gene expression at early time points in YOD1 knock-down cells (Figure 4F).

claim: p62 exerts a dual role by first activating TRAF6 and later recruiting CYLD.
source: Since p62 exerts a dual role by first activating TRAF6 and later recruiting CYLD (Sanz et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2008), CYLD may at least partially impede enhanced signaling upon loss of YOD1 during an IL-1 response.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Sanz et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2008).

claim: CYLD may at least partially impede enhanced signaling upon loss of YOD1 during an IL-1 response.
source: Since p62 exerts a dual role by first activating TRAF6 and later recruiting CYLD (Sanz et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2008), CYLD may at least partially impede enhanced signaling upon loss of YOD1 during an IL-1 response.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the dual role of p62 and the timing of CYLD action.

claim: YOD1 depletion had no significant influence on IL-1-induced MAPK activation.
source: YOD1 depletion had no significant influence on IL-1-induced MAPK activation, even though TRAF6 is controlling p38 and JNK activation upon IL-1R engagement (Lamothe et al., 2008; Ortis et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of MAPK phosphorylation in YOD1 knock-down cells (Figure 6E) and supported by citations (Lamothe et al., 2008; Ortis et al., 2012).

claim: p62 is not substantially involved in the activation of JNK by TRAF6.
source: However, despite its role in NF-κB signaling, p62 is not substantially involved in the activation of JNK by TRAF6 (Sanz et al., 2000; Feng and Longmore, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Sanz et al., 2000; Feng and Longmore, 2005).

claim: Normal JNK signaling in YOD1 knock-down cells supports the notion that YOD1 is selectively acting on p62/TRAF6 complexes.
source: Thus, normal JNK signaling in YOD1 knock-down cells further supports the notion that YOD1 is selectively acting on p62/TRAF6 complexes.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect on MAPK activation (Figure 6E) combined with p62's lack of involvement in JNK activation.

claim: TRAF6 activation of MAPK and NF-κB signaling involves different subsets of TRAF6 interactors.
source: Hence, TRAF6 activation of MAPK and NF-κB signaling seems to involve different subsets of TRAF6 interactors.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of YOD1 on NF-κB versus MAPK signaling.

claim: The TRAF6/p62 signaling axis mediates NF-κB activation in response to CD40, RANK or NGF stimulation.
source: The TRAF6/p62 signaling axis was shown to also mediate NF-κB activation in response to other inducers, including CD40, RANK or NGF stimulation (Wooten et al., 2005; Durán et al., 2004; Seibold and Ehrenschwender, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Wooten et al., 2005; Durán et al., 2004; Seibold and Ehrenschwender, 2015).

claim: YOD1 knock-down does not enhance NF-κB signaling upon CD40 or RANK stimulation in 293 or PC3 cells.
source: Quite unexpectedly, we did not observe enhanced NF-κB signaling after YOD1 knock-down upon CD40 or RANK stimulation in 293 or PC3 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA and Western blot in YOD1 knock-down cells stimulated with CD40-L or RANKL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).

claim: NF-κB activation is impaired upon decreased YOD1 expression after CD40 or RANK stimulation in 293 or PC3 cells.
source: In contrast, NF-κB activation was even impaired upon decreased YOD1 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA and Western blot in YOD1 knock-down cells stimulated with CD40-L or RANKL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).

claim: p62 knock-down does not significantly influence CD40 and RANK signaling in 293 or PC3 cells.
source: However, in this cellular context p62 knock-down did not significantly influence CD40 and RANK signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA and Western blot in p62 knock-down cells stimulated with CD40-L or RANKL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).

claim: CD40-induced NF-κB signaling was weakened in macrophages from p62-mutant mice but unaffected in a human kidney tumor cell line after p62 knock-down.
source: Previously, Seibold et al reported that CD40-induced NF-κB signaling was weakend in macrophages from p62-mutant mice, but unaffected in a human kidney tumor cell line after p62 knock-down (Seibold and Ehrenschwender, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Seibold and Ehrenschwender, 2015).

claim: p62 is dispensable for immediate early NF-κB signaling in response to RANK and only controls a second wave of NF-κB activity in osteoclasts after several days of stimulation.
source: Further, p62 was shown to be dispensable for immediate early NF-κB signaling in response to RANK and it only controlled a second wave of NF-κB activity in osteoclasts after several days of stimulation (Durán et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Durán et al., 2004).

claim: The role of p62 for different TRAF6-dependent signaling pathways is stimulation, cell-type and context-dependent.
source: Apparently, the results reveal a stimulation, cell-type and context-dependent role of p62 for different TRAF6-dependent signaling pathways, which may explain why YOD1 is not acting as a general negative regulator in all these settings.
evidence: Inferred from variable effects of p62 in different cellular contexts as reported in literature and observed in experiments.

claim: YOD1 was originally identified as a co-factor of p97 in the regulation of protein quality control and the ERAD pathway.
source: Of note, YOD1 was originally identified as a co-factor of p97 in the regulation of protein quality control and the ERAD pathway (Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006; Ernst et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006; Ernst et al., 2009).

claim: YOD1/TRAF6 binding is independent of p97.
source: YOD1/TRAF6 binding is apparently independent of p97, suggesting that YOD1 affects NF-κB signaling in response to IL-1 independent of this multifunctional AAA-ATPase.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in p97 knock-down cells showing no effect on YOD1/TRAF6 interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).

claim: p97 positively regulates canonical NF-κB signaling by facilitating proteasomal IκBα degradation.
source: However, p97 was shown to positively regulate canonical NF-κB signaling by facilitating proteasomal IκBα degradation (Li et al., 2014; Schweitzer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Li et al., 2014; Schweitzer et al., 2016).

claim: YOD1 deficiency alone is not sufficient to induce TRAF6 ubiquitination or IKK/NF-κB signaling in the absence of stimulation.
source: Clearly, YOD1 deficiency alone is not sufficient to induce TRAF6 ubiquitination or IKK/NF-κB signaling in the absence of any stimulation.
evidence: Observed in YOD1 KO cells without stimulation.

claim: Changes in TRAF6 expression and TRAF6 oligomerization can activate downstream signaling.
source: However, changes in TRAF6 expression and TRAF6 oligomerization can activate downstream signaling (Cao et al., 1996; Baud et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Cao et al., 1996; Baud et al., 1999).

claim: The C-terminal MATH of TRAF6 is an oligomerization and interaction domain.
source: The C-terminal MATH of TRAF6 is an oligomerization and interaction domain (Arch et al., 1998; Ha et al., 2009) and stimulus-dependent recruitment of many adaptors including p62 is mediated by a consensus TRAF6 interaction motif (TIM) (Ye et al., 2002; Linares et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Arch et al., 1998; Ha et al., 2009).

claim: Stimulus-dependent recruitment of many adaptors including p62 is mediated by a consensus TRAF6 interaction motif (TIM).
source: The C-terminal MATH of TRAF6 is an oligomerization and interaction domain (Arch et al., 1998; Ha et al., 2009) and stimulus-dependent recruitment of many adaptors including p62 is mediated by a consensus TRAF6 interaction motif (TIM) (Ye et al., 2002; Linares et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Ye et al., 2002; Linares et al., 2013).

claim: The putative TIM of YOD1 is not required for binding to the TRAF6 MATH domain.
source: The putative TIM of YOD1 is not required for binding to the TRAF6 MATH domain, indicating a different binding mode of YOD1 in un-induced cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments showing mutations in the putative TIM do not abolish YOD1/TRAF6 binding (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).

claim: YOD1 specifically binds to TRAF6 and not to TRAF2.
source: Nevertheless, YOD1 specifically binds to TRAF6 and not to TRAF2, and consequently YOD1 counteracts TRAF6-dependent NF-κB signaling from the IL-1R and not the TNFR.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation showing no YOD1-TRAF2 binding (Figure 1G) and EMSA showing no effect on TNFα signaling (Figure 6F).

claim: YOD1 counteracts TRAF6-dependent NF-κB signaling from the IL-1R and not the TNFR.
source: Nevertheless, YOD1 specifically binds to TRAF6 and not to TRAF2, and consequently YOD1 counteracts TRAF6-dependent NF-κB signaling from the IL-1R and not the TNFR.
evidence: Demonstrated by differential effects of YOD1 knock-down on IL-1β versus TNFα signaling (Figure 6F).

claim: YOD1/TRAF6 interaction takes place in unstimulated cells indicating that TRAF6 oligomerization is not required.
source: Since YOD1/TRAF6 interaction takes place in unstimulated cells, TRAF6 oligomerization is apparently not required, indicating that monomeric TRAF6 has a preference for binding to YOD1 over p62.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in unstimulated cells (Figure 1H-K, Figure 7C, 7D).

claim: Monomeric TRAF6 has a preference for binding to YOD1 over p62.
source: Since YOD1/TRAF6 interaction takes place in unstimulated cells, TRAF6 oligomerization is apparently not required, indicating that monomeric TRAF6 has a preference for binding to YOD1 over p62.
evidence: Inferred from YOD1 binding in unstimulated cells and competitive binding with p62.

claim: YOD1 raises the threshold for TRAF6/p62 signaling to occur.
source: Whether this is due to higher affinity or localization inside the cell needs to be elaborated, but the data suggest that YOD1 raises the threshold for TRAF6/p62 signaling to occur.
evidence: Inferred from YOD1's ability to compete with p62 and prevent TRAF6 activation in unstimulated cells.

claim: The C-terminal MATH domain of TRAF6 associates with TIMs in various adaptors to regulate signaling in different settings.
source: The C-terminal MATH domain of TRAF6 associates with TIMs in various adaptors to regulate signaling in different settings. These adapters include MALT1 and Caspase8 in activated T cells (Sun et al., 2004; Oeckinghaus et al., 2007; Bidère et al., 2006), TIFA after IL-1 stimulation (Takatsuna et al., 2003; Ea et al., 2004) or TRIP6 in lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) stimulated cells (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Sun et al., 2004; Oeckinghaus et al., 2007; Bidère et al., 2006; Takatsuna et al., 2003; Ea et al., 2004; Lin et al., 2016).

claim: TRAF6 recruitment to p62 sequestosomes is enhanced upon IL-1β stimulation.
source: TRAF6 recruitment to p62 sequestosomes is enhanced upon IL-1β stimulation (Sanz et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Sanz et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2010).

claim: Sequestosomes are hotspots for signal transduction activity and can contribute to proteasomal degradation by co-localizing with the proteasome.
source: Sequestosomes are hotspots for signal transduction activity and in addition they can contribute to proteasomal degradation by co-localizing with the proteasome (Seibenhener et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Seibenhener et al., 2004).

claim: Freshly formed sequestosomes constitute a microenvironment for signaling to boost NF-κB activation.
source: Hence, freshly formed sequestosomes constitute a microenvironment for signaling to boost NF-κB activation (Seibenhener et al., 2004; Sanz et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Seibenhener et al., 2004; Sanz et al., 2000).

claim: In the course of prolonged stimulation, sequestosomes mature into proteasome-organizing centers and NF-κB signaling is terminated.
source: In the course of prolonged stimulation, sequestosomes mature into proteasome-organizing centers and NF-κB signaling is terminated (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Wang et al., 2010).

claim: YOD1 is able to counteract TRAF6 recruitment to sequestosomes and NF-κB signaling.
source: Our data indicate that YOD1 is able to counteract TRAF6 recruitment to sequestosomes and NF-κB signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy showing YOD1 prevents TRAF6 recruitment to p62 aggregates (Figure 3F) and functional assays showing reduced NF-κB signaling (Figure 4C, Figure 5E-F).
